To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

DL(CO) decreased and LTV increased in sitting subjects in G(z+) because blood is sequestered in the dependent part and the distribution of alveoli and capillaries is less homogenous than under normal gravity.
lung diffusing capacity decreases in parallel with lung tissue volume during hypergravity, indicating that the lung is a gravity-dependent organ.

the lung diffusing capacity for CO (DL(CO)), which is mainly determined by the diffusing capacity of its membrane component, decreases in sitting subjects during head-to-feet hypergravity due to a less homogenous pulmonary capillary blood distribution, while lung tissue volume, including pulmonary capillary volume, increases due to peripheral pooling.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of hypergravity and hypogravity on the pulmonary gas exchange.
the effects of gravity on the lung.
the effects of hypergravity on the pulmonary diffusing capacity in humans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hypergravity causes a redistribution of blood in the lung, with a reduction of the central and an increase of the peripheral blood volume.
the lung behaves as a peripheral vascular organ, but that the distribution of alveoli and pulmonary capillaries is not uniform.
the pulmonary circulation is not a simple passive system but is able to react with an increase in LTV in hypergravity, which is probably an important compensatory mechanism in the lung.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pulmonary circulation is not as sensitive to gravity as the systemic circulation.
DL(CO) decreased with increasing hypergravity, whereas LTV increased, indicating that DL(CO)/LTV is a more stable parameter than DL(CO) or LTV alone.
the lung is not an exception in the hypergravity situation but behaves in the same way as the systemic circulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DL(CO) does not change in concert with LTV in hypergravity.
the changes in DL(CO) are not necessarily a reflection of changes in LTV.
the lung is a complex system, where changes in one component (e.g., pulmonary capillary blood flow) do not necessarily lead to changes in other components (e.g., DL(CO)).
